prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery-grade invention with a clear mechanism: Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, while being interrogated in parallel. Ye's JILA work then showed what this buys, with fractional uncertainty in the 10^-18 range, coherence and many-body control, and direct observation of gravitational redshift over millimetre scales. Independent laboratories on several species reproduce the performance and compare clocks across continents. Applications reach well beyond timekeeping, into relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signatures, and a prospective redefinition of the second. The credited pair is clean and matches the intellectual history, with no forced exclusion of a principal. Colleagues rank it first (Kroll), second (Eriksson) and in the top three (Danielsson, Olsson, Pearce), and it carries the broadest support on the shortlist, though I do not treat support as merit. My reason is that the physics is sharp, the impact is demonstrated by measurement, and the attribution is the least contested of the shortlisted candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier prizes: frequency combs (2005) and ion control and ion clocks (2012) already honoured the enabling technology and a neighbouring clock platform, so the committee may see the lattice clock as a refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery. A related point is timing, since the second has not yet been redefined and some will want to wait for that. Others who made key early measurements or developed the supporting laser stabilisation and comparison techniques, such as the groups at PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo, are outside a two-name credit, and my recollection of early priority details has not been checked here. Finally, metrology prizes can read as instrument achievements, and the citation must make clear that the new element is the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B052 only seventh, noting that frequency combs were honoured in 2005 and that the recognition could be timed to the expected redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but think it is answered by the physics. Combs gave a way to count optical cycles. The lattice clock solves a different problem, namely how to interrogate many neutral atoms with no first-order Doppler, recoil or light-shift error, and that is what gave stability and accuracy beyond what single-ion clocks can reach in practical averaging time. On timing, I would not tie a prize to a metrological decision. The performance is already confirmed by many independent groups, and waiting for the redefinition would add nothing to the scientific case. Where I agree with Mehlig is that the citation must be narrow, naming the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realisation, so that it does not read as a general prize for optical clocks.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs experimental discovery (B010) first, as the unrecognised experimental half of a story closed by the 2013 prize, and accepts that the named trio is a defensible but imperfect choice.
responses.response: I agree the Higgs discovery is scientifically beyond doubt and that the 2013 prize left the experimental half open. My difficulty is attribution. Pearce himself says the founding spokespersons did not make the 2012 analysis decisions, and the prize would be for a discovery by thousands of people. I would be uneasy giving the committee's only slot this year to a configuration we would struggle to defend on the evidence. By contrast, in B052 the individuals named are those who proposed and realised the key step. I would not rule B010 out, but its attribution problem is much more serious than anything in the lattice-clock case, and I would want a clear argument for why these three and not the analysis or detector-technology leaders.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B021) first, as a new classification of electronic phases with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Hasan are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I share Eriksson's view that topological insulators are a major and mature field, and it is my third choice. The point he raises about missing names is, in my view, the decisive weakness. If the HgTe observation followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D materials work involved others, then the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio would leave out people whose contribution was necessary, and the 2016 prize on topological phases already touches the theme. I would support B021 only if the committee were confident of a defensible three-name allocation, which the supplied credit does not give. That is the main reason I place the clock ahead of it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B052 first as a clean two-person configuration, with Katori proposing the lattice scheme and Ye driving the record stability, while noting that others such as Takamoto and Lemonde contributed to the ecosystem.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the credit and on timing. I would add one qualification to his list: Takamoto's strontium clock demonstration, the PTB, SYRTE and NIST contributions, and the Hall-era laser-stabilisation work show that the credit is clean for the lattice-clock concept and its performance record, but not for every clock result. I would therefore keep the citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and the demonstrations of record accuracy, and not extend it to optical clocks in general. That wording protects the two-name configuration from the objection that others were left out.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether a narrowly framed citation is enough to answer it.

Whether other early lattice-clock contributors, such as Takamoto or groups at PTB, SYRTE and NIST, should be recognised, which the two-name credit does not allow; I recall the priority details from memory and have not verified them here.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.

The attribution of the topological-insulator and quantum-simulation alternatives (missing theorists; Esslinger versus Zoller) is not resolved by the supplied names, so my fallback ranking is provisional.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B052 is apparent from my profile: Katori and Ye are not among my documented collaborators. My documented connections are to Ingvar Lindgren's group, Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom appear in the shortlist credits. I do share the atomic physics field with the lattice-clock work, which I note as expertise rather than a conflict.
